# Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basins in Autoresearch Agents

Ziyang Cai^(\*)    Christos Ziakas^(\*)    Vasilis Kontonis    Tim
Pearce Affiliation: Siddhartha Sen   Akshay Krishnamurthy   Shivam Garg
  Dimitris Papailiopoulos Affiliation: Microsoft Research

###### Abstract

Autoresearch agents tackle open-ended problems by repeatedly proposing
candidate solutions, evaluating them, and using feedback to guide
subsequent experiments. We show that independent runs of the same agent
on the same task often plateau at substantially different scores, with
gaps that persist even after considerable additional compute. Embedding
their candidate artifacts by functional similarity provides further
evidence that trajectories remain in localized regions of the solution
space, which we call _idea basins_. To help agents escape these basins,
we study a simple periodic intervention, _fork-and-flush_. Our method
forks the agent into parallel trajectories, each inheriting the
accumulated workspace but starting with a fresh chat context. After
running each trajectory for a fixed horizon, the agent continues from
the highest-scoring one. Across $`13`$ long-horizon research and
engineering tasks, with individual agent runs lasting up to several
days, _fork-and-flush_ outperformed the single-run and best-of-$`N`$
baselines by a relative improvement of $`66.0\%`$ and $`44.4\%`$,
respectively, on the min–max normalized average score under an equal
compute budget.

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Eight independent agents on p171 research task. Left:
Best-so-far score against compute spend, with dots representing

Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shown remarkable promise in
autonomously solving hard, open-ended research problems requiring long
execution horizons ([Mang et al., 2026](#bib.bib16); [Merrill et al.,
2026](#bib.bib14); [Terminal-Bench-Science Team, 2026](#bib.bib15)). A
prominent paradigm for addressing these problems is the _autoresearch_
loop ([Karpathy, 2026](#bib.bib6); [Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib7)),
where an agent iteratively proposes a solution, evaluates it within an
environment, and uses the execution feedback or submission score to
guide its next experiment. This process can be viewed loosely as _idea
descent_, by analogy with gradient descent: feedback guides successive
modifications through the space of candidate solutions. Consider, for
example, the task of finding the smallest CIFAR classifier that achieves
a target accuracy. Although the objective is easy to state, the design
space is broad: the agent can explore different architecture families,
layer depths and widths, computational blocks, and training recipes,
with many possible tradeoffs between accuracy and model size. A single
autoresearch run can evaluate hundreds of candidate solutions and
continue for multiple days. This scale raises a fundamental question:
over such long horizons, does an agent explore the solution space
broadly, or does it mainly refine the ideas it selected early on?

We first examine how solution quality evolves over long autoresearch
runs. The score of the best solution found so far tends to plateau
within a run. More revealingly, independent runs of the same agent on
the same task plateau at substantially different levels, with gaps that
persist even after considerable additional compute
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")).
This suggests that runs may differ not just in how quickly they improve,
but in which parts of the solution space they explore. To investigate
this possibility, we embed their candidate artifacts in two dimensions
based on functional similarity
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")).
The resulting visualization provides additional evidence: submissions
from individual runs tend to remain in localized regions of this space.
Continuing the _idea descent_ analogy, we call these regions _idea
basins_. Some runs appear to spend much of their subsequent effort
refining solutions in less productive regions rather than discovering
the higher-scoring solutions found by other runs. Notably, this
localization persists despite periodic compaction of the agents’
conversational histories.

Can we exploit the variation across independent runs to improve an
ongoing run by encouraging it to explore more broadly? To this end, we
consider two natural operations that are easy to incorporate into
existing autoresearch loops. _Forking_ lets the agent try several
candidate continuations and select one based on their scores. _Flushing_
clears the inherited chat history while retaining the accumulated
workspace, allowing the continuations to explore with less dependence on
earlier reasoning. Our intervention, _fork-and-flush_, combines these
operations periodically: it forks the agent into parallel trajectories
that each inherit a copy of the current workspace and begin with a fresh
chat context, runs each for a fixed horizon, and continues from the
highest-scoring trajectory.

We evaluate _fork-and-flush_ across 13 long-horizon research and
engineering tasks
(Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix B Task descriptions ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")).
Eleven are drawn from Frontier-CS ([Mang et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)) and
EdgeBench ([Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)), spanning problems from
polyomino packing and job-shop scheduling to cryptanalysis and inferring
a groundwater contaminant source from well readings. The remaining two
tasks involve designing a compact CIFAR classifier under an accuracy
constraint and optimizing a kernel for a simulated VLIW machine.
Individual agent runs last from several hours to multiple days depending
on the task. Under an equal compute budget, _fork-and-flush_ outperforms
both the single-run and best-of-$`N`$ baselines, achieving $`66.0\%`$
and $`44.4\%`$ relative improvements in min–max normalized average
score, respectively. Our artifact embedding also shows broader
exploration under fork-and-flush
(Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")),
connecting the gains to the idea-basin observation.

We summarize our key contributions as follows:

- •
  We show that long-running autoresearch agents exhibit persistent
  outcome variance: independent runs on the same task plateau at
  substantially different scores, with gaps that remain even after
  considerable additional compute.
- •
  We show that a simple intervention, _fork-and-flush_, improves
  performance by periodically forking and flushing the chat context
  while preserving accumulated work. In an evaluation across 13
  open-ended tasks, including research and applied engineering
  challenges with individual runs lasting up to 107 hours, it
  outperforms single-run and best-of-$`N`$ baselines under equal compute
  budgets.
- •
  We develop an embedding of agent artifacts based on functional
  similarity to study where trajectories search. It reveals localized
  exploration consistent with _idea basins_ and shows broader movement
  through this space under _fork-and-flush_.

Figure 2: An illustration of _fork-and-flush_. Left: A single run (grey,
dashed) keeps exploring similar ideas within one basin. Fork-and-flush
clears the chat context on the same workspace ($`\diamond`$), fans out
$`K`$ probes, retains the best ($`\star`$), and discards the rest
($`\times`$). Right: While the leader’s edits remain localized, a
fresh-context probe jumps to a new basin via fork-and-flush and

## 2 Preliminaries: Autoresearch Setup

Open-ended Research Tasks. We evaluate on thirteen diverse open-ended
tasks spanning algorithmic optimization, cryptanalysis, scientific
inference, and systems engineering
(Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix B Task descriptions ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")).
Nine are drawn from Frontier-CS ([Mang et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)),
including four classical algorithmic challenges (polyomino, job-shop,
sphere-pack, relay-lay), three AtCoder competitive programming ports
(AHC014, p150, p171), one cache optimization research task (LLM-SQL),
and one cryptanalysis challenge (LWE-rec). Two tasks come from
EdgeBench ([Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)), targeting groundwater source
recovery (Borden-inv) and black-box permutation optimization
(order-add). The remaining two are large-budget engineering problems,
specifically Anthropic’s public VLIW optimization take-home
(kernel) ([Anthropic, 2026](#bib.bib29)) and a custom CIFAR model
compression task (tinyCIFAR). Performance is evaluated using verifiable,
deterministic metrics tailored to each domain, providing an unbounded
signal for continuous improvement. Because these raw scores use
task-specific scales, measuring outcome variance and comparing
interventions requires multiple independent trajectories on each task.
Per-run budgets range from $`6{,}000`$ to $`100{,}000`$ GitHub Copilot
CLI credits, with individual runs lasting from several hours to multiple
days. Full task descriptions are provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Task descriptions ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents").

Autoresearch Harness. An agent harness enables the interaction between
an LLM agent and an isolated container environment ([Falck et al.,
2026](#bib.bib35)). In our autoresearch setup ([Karpathy,
2026](#bib.bib6)), the agent’s execution proceeds as a sequence of
submission episodes including editing, execution, and evaluation in a
loop; within an episode, the agent edits its solver, runs it, and
submits for a score as often as it chooses. These episodes terminate
upon a self-halting action by the agent or by reaching a predefined
token budget. Upon the conclusion of an episode, our autoresearch
harness resumes the agent via a short continuation prompt. Across these
episodes, both the _workspace_ $`W`$, consisting of the files it has
produced, and the _conversational context_ $`C`$, its accumulated chat
history, are strictly preserved, and interventions occur only at episode
boundaries. We define a state as $`s_{i}=(W_{i},C_{i})`$ and a _lineage_
$`\ell=(s_{0},\dots,s_{t})`$ as the trajectory of these states, starting
from an empty base state $`s_{0}=(\emptyset,\emptyset)`$. At each step,
a deterministic grader evaluates the workspace to yield a score
$`f(W_{i})`$, and we let $`J(\ell)=\max_{i}f(W_{i})`$ denote the maximum
objective score achieved by this lineage. For a given task with a fixed
total compute budget $`B`$, measured in compute _credits_, a fixed
function of input/output model tokens ($`100`$ credits $`\approx`$
US\$1), the final result is the maximum score discovered by an
autoresearch agent across a long-horizon run
$`R=\max_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}J(\ell)`$, where $`\mathcal{L}`$ represents
the set of all lineages instantiated by the method within budget $`B`$.
All conditions use the same coding agent, GitHub Copilot CLI (version
1.0.73), with the same tools, prompt, and task workspace.

## 3 Idea Basins in Autoresearch

Persistent Variance. We begin by examining independent autoresearch runs
on a single task.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")
(left) shows the best score found so far by eight runs on p171. Although
the runs share the same initial state and underlying model, they plateau
for long stretches at substantially different levels. Their final best
scores range from 68.3 to 100.0, and the gaps remain wide even after
considerable additional compute. The combination of within-run plateaus
and persistent between-run variation suggests that the runs differ not
just in how quickly they improve, but also in which parts of the
solution space they explore. Some appear to spend much of their
remaining compute refining less promising approaches without reaching
the higher-scoring approaches found by other runs. In
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Variance Analysis Plots ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents"),
we provide additional plots demonstrating this wide spread of
independent runs on four further tasks.

Idea Basins. A submission may be a complex program, and its score tells
us little about how it relates to other submissions. Can we visualize
these relationships to see what an agent explores as its score plateaus?
To do so, we ask an LLM to compare artifacts in triplets: given an
anchor artifact $`a`$ and two candidates $`b`$ and $`c`$, which
candidate takes an approach more similar to $`a`$? We then seek a
two-dimensional map that respects these relative comparisons. To
construct the triplets, we collect graded submissions, remove exact
duplicates by content hash, and subsample up to $`51`$ evenly spaced
artifacts per run. Before comparison, we rewrite each artifact as a
functional specification under a fixed schema. This reduces cues from
code syntax and shared scaffolding that might make submissions from the
same run look similar for reasons unrelated to their approach. We fit
the map using t-distributed stochastic triplet embedding (t-STE) ([van
der Maaten and Weinberger, 2012](#bib.bib28)).

The map captures substantial structure in the LLM’s similarity
judgments. Across five mapped tasks, it agrees with $`85\%`$ of held-out
triplet judgments on average, compared with $`50\%`$ for chance and
$`56\%`$ for a heuristic that knows only which run produced each
artifact.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")
(right) shows the map for p171. Submissions from individual runs tend to
concentrate in localized regions, which we call _idea basins_. The
shaded regions show $`k`$-means clusters fitted to baseline artifacts.
Later submissions generally remain near the same region, providing a
view of the repeated refinement suggested by the score plateaus. To test
whether this clustered pattern depends on our choice of t-STE, we repeat
the mapping using Soft Ordinal Embedding (SOE) ([Terada and von Luxburg,
2014](#bib.bib4)), achieving a mean held-out agreement of $`0.83`$. In
addition, the observed clustering of idea basins qualitatively remains
the same under SOE, albeit with less sharp boundaries, as described in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Robustness of the Embedding Space ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents").
The full mapping pipeline and the validation of both embeddings are
detailed in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Artifact Embedding Methodology ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents").
In the following sections, we introduce the _fork-and-flush_
intervention and use the same map to show how it helps trajectories move
between idea basins.

## 4 Escaping Idea Basins via Fork-and-flush

Problem Setup. Open-ended research problems present a combinatorially
large solution space, resulting in significant outcome variance across
agent trajectories, as empirically shown in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Idea Basins in Autoresearch ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents").
This raises a natural question: can we leverage the variance observed
across independent runs to help an ongoing trajectory escape its current
basin? Committing a global budget $`B`$ entirely to a single run (pure
exploitation) often leads the agent to settle into one basin early and
spend the remaining budget on marginal refinements. Conversely, parallel
scaling approaches like best-of-$`N`$ ([Snell et al., 2024](#bib.bib5))
represent pure exploration: $`N`$ independent runs of budget $`B/N`$
sample diverse basins, but the individual runs remain shallow, and the
accumulated workspaces of the $`N{-}1`$ discarded runs are completely
wasted. Interleaved forking provides a natural interpolation between
these extremes. A process that never branches is a single run; one that
branches exactly once from an empty workspace and terminates is
best-of-$`N`$. To actively exploit this variance to escape idea basins,
we introduce an approach that alternates between parallel sampling and
serial execution, driven by two core mechanisms: forking and flushing.

Forking and Flushing. Our method relies on two underlying mechanisms to
escape idea basins. First, _forking_ creates $`K`$ parallel agents
$`\ell^{1},\dots,\ell^{K}`$. Each branch inherits the current lineage
and is allocated an exploration budget $`b_{\text{explore}}`$. Upon
exhausting this budget, the highest-scoring branch
$`\ell^{\star}=\arg\max_{k}J(\ell^{k})`$ is selected, and the remaining
branches are discarded. Forking places $`K`$ probes into the search
space simultaneously, allowing the selection mechanism to choose between
basins rather than refining within just one. Second, _flushing_ retains
the accumulated workspace but flushes the conversational context:
$`(W,C)\to(W,\emptyset)`$. A branch that retained $`C`$ would carry the
parent’s reasoning that tends to re-enter the same local basin. Starting
from $`(W,\emptyset)`$ restores search diversity while preserving the
accumulated workspace.

The Fork-and-flush Algorithm. The proposed algorithm alternates between
exploration and exploitation on a fixed schedule as shown in
Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents").
It begins with an initial round of forking from empty workspaces: $`K`$
agents each receive $`b_{\text{explore}}`$, and the highest-scoring one
is selected as the _leader_. The leader then continues alone until it
exhausts an exploitative budget $`b_{\text{exploit}}`$. At that trigger
point, the algorithm initiates a fork coupled with a flush: $`K`$ new
parallel agents start from the current workspace $`(W_{t},\emptyset)`$,
and each is granted $`b_{\text{explore}}`$. When the round closes, the
best branch is selected as the new leader, the others are pruned, and
the run continues sequentially from the new trunk. This loop repeats
until the global budget $`B`$ is exhausted. The run’s final result is
the best score found by any agent throughout the trajectory. In
Section [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Ablations: Impact of Forking and Flushing ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents"),
we conduct ablation studies to isolate the independent contributions of
forking and flushing. We opt for a fixed schedule to trigger
_fork-and-flush_ rather than dynamic plateau detection; full details on
this design choice and its sensitivity are provided in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Schedule Design ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents").

## 5 Experiments

### 5.1 Experimental Setup

Baselines. We compare our method against two strategies under strictly
matched global budgets. The _single-run_ baseline spends the full budget
$`B`$ sequentially on a single lineage; we execute eight independent
single-run baselines per task. The _best-of-$`N`$_ baseline ($`N{=}4`$)
distributes the budget equally, allocating $`B/4`$ to each of four
independent runs and keeping the best final result.

Evaluation Setup. Each task is allocated a fixed per-run compute budget
$`B`$, as detailed in
Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix B Task descriptions ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents").
Within a given task, all conditions utilize the identical underlying
agent model: GPT-5.6-terra at high reasoning effort for eleven tasks,
and GPT-5.5 at extra-high reasoning effort for kernel and tinyCIFAR.
Each task is evaluated across five independent fork-and-flush runs. We
report the maximum, mean, and standard deviation of final scores for
each task, alongside a min–max normalized average across all thirteen
tasks.

Fork-and-Flush Configuration. Every _fork-and-flush_ run in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Escaping Idea Basins via Fork-and-flush ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")
adheres to a fixed forced cadence featuring three fan-outs, removing the
need for fragile plateau detection. The run opens with an initial round
of $`K{=}4`$ agents launched from empty workspaces, selecting the
highest-scoring candidate as the leader. Two subsequent fork-and-flush
rounds are triggered strictly by budget consumption—at $`33\%`$ and
$`66\%`$ of $`B`$. In these rounds, $`K{=}4`$ new branches fork from the
leader’s accumulated workspace but begin with empty chat contexts. Each
branch receives a fixed exploration budget $`b_{\text{explore}}`$ of
approximately $`0.06B`$; the best-performing branch is adopted as the
new leader, the others are discarded, and the leader continues serially
until the next trigger. We provide a detailed analysis of this schedule
design and its hyperparameter sensitivity in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Schedule Design ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents").

### 5.2 Main Results

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Escaping Idea Basins via Fork-and-flush ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")
compares final performance under matched compute budgets.
_Fork-and-flush_ achieves a min–max normalized average score of
$`0.78`$, compared with $`0.47`$ for _single-run_ and $`0.54`$ for
_best-of-4_, representing relative improvements of $`66.0\%`$ and
$`44.4\%`$, respectively. These gains extend across the task suite:
_fork-and-flush_ achieves the highest mean score on 12 of the 13 tasks.
Across tasks, its average normalized _mean_ score ($`0.78`$) exceeds
even the average normalized _maximum_ score of the single-run baseline
($`0.75`$). Alongside these performance gains, _fork-and-flush_ produces
more consistent outcomes on average. The average normalized standard
deviation decreases to $`0.16`$, compared with $`0.26`$ for _single-run_
and $`0.21`$ for _best-of-4_. Relative to _single-run_, the standard
deviation decreases on 10 of the 13 tasks. Variability increases on some
tasks, including AHC014 and order-add, where these increases accompany
substantial gains in mean score. Their larger raw standard deviations
should therefore be interpreted alongside the higher score levels
reached. Overall, _fork-and-flush_ combines substantial improvements in
average performance with greater consistency across independent runs.

| Method         | Flush      | Fork       | Norm. avg         |
| -------------- | ---------- | ---------- | ----------------- |
| Single-run     | $`\times`$ | $`\times`$ | $`0.45`$          |
| Flushing       | ✓          | $`\times`$ | $`0.55`$          |
| Forking        | $`\times`$ | ✓          | $`\mathit{0.57}`$ |
| Fork-and-flush | ✓          | ✓          | $`\mathbf{0.71}`$ |

Table 2: Impact of forking and flushing: min–max normalized mean score
over 11 tasks. Best in bold, second best in _italics_.

### 5.3 Ablations: Impact of Forking and Flushing

To isolate the contributions of our core mechanisms, we evaluate the
impact of forking without flushing the context, and flushing the context
without forking across 11 tasks (excluding the two longest-horizon tasks
that are expensive to run). In
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents"),
we report the performance of all four methods as the min–max normalized
final score at the task’s budget, averaged across all tasks. The
flush-only and fork-only ablations achieve scores of 0.55 and 0.57
respectively, compared to 0.45 for the standard single-run baseline, and
0.71 for the full _fork-and-flush_ method. This demonstrates that while
both individual components outperform the single-run baseline, neither
mechanism alone accounts for the full effect. In addition, forking
provides a slightly larger improvement than flushing. The complete
per-task breakdown is provided in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Ablation: Full Results ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents").

## 6 Analysis

### 6.1 Visualizing Escaping Idea Basins

Figure 3: Fork-and-flush escaping an idea basin on polyomino. Left: A
mid-run fan-out overlaid on baseline basins. Rejected branches
($`\times`$) from the fork point ($`\diamond`$) remain trapped, but the
selected branch (blue arrow) escapes the idea basin to achieve its final
score ($`\star`$). Right: Step distances between consecutive
submissions. The selected branch’s jump ($`\star`$) cleanly breaks out
of the standard single-run refinement range (grey band).

Visualizing the Jump. We place the artifacts of fork-and-flush runs on
the same geometric maps built in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Idea Basins in Autoresearch ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents"),
embedded jointly with the single-run baselines so that both share an
embedding space, enabling fork-and-flush to be interpreted as a spatial
trajectory across the solution landscape. As illustrated in
Figure [3](#S6.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 6.1 Visualizing Escaping Idea Basins ‣ 6 Analysis ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")
(left), we overlay the mid-run fan-out of a _fork-and-flush_ trajectory
on the polyomino task. While leader edits remain highly localized, the
intervention successfully forces exploration: branches $`b_{1}`$,
$`b_{2}`$, and $`b_{4}`$ remain trapped in the basin of the branch
point, but the fresh-context probe $`b_{3}`$ successfully jumps into a
new region (Basin 3). This probe is selected by the scoring mechanism,
allowing the run to escape the local optimum and finish at $`93.9`$. We
provide additional plots showing these jumps in
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Trajectories Across Idea Basins ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents").

Quantifying the Jump. To quantify the jump, we report distances in units
of the _median single-run step_, defined as the median displacement
between consecutive submissions across all single-run baselines. On
polyomino, after the first quarter of the budget, no single run moves
more than $`4.4`$ units between consecutive submissions, and the
fork-and-flush leader’s own sequential steps stay within $`2.9`$ units.
At the flush fan-out (triggered at $`71\%`$ of the budget), the winning
branch ($`b_{3}`$) moves $`43`$ units in its very first submission after
the flush, definitively landing in a different basin; the three rejected
branches each move at most one unit and stay where they forked. Once
established in the new basin, the leader’s refinement steps drop back to
the single-run scale (at most $`5.2`$ units, an order of magnitude below
the jump).

Robustness of the Jump. We provide an additional analysis using SOE to
fit the embedding space in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Robustness of the Embedding Space ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents").
In our analysis, the qualitative pattern remains identical, confirming
the jump is a genuine artifact of our search strategy and robust to the
triplet embedding method. In particular, under SOE, no single run moves
more than $`4.1`$ units between consecutive submissions. At the flush
fan-out, the three rejected branches each move under one unit, while the
winning branch moves $`10.1`$ units in its first submission after the
flush into a different cluster; its subsequent steps then fall back
inside the single-run range.

### 6.2 What Drives Variance?

Variance at the capability frontier. Our hypothesis is that outcome
variance is driven by task difficulty relative to the agent’s capacity.
When a task sits far below the agent’s ability, every run finds the same
optimal solution and the spread collapses. Conversely, when a task sits
far above its capacity, every run fails in the same way, collapsing the
spread again. It is only in the intermediate regime—at the exact
boundary of what the agent can achieve—that runs make partial, divergent
progress, maximizing variance. A natural assumption is that as
foundational models scale and become stronger, they will solve current
tasks reliably and this variance will vanish. However, we expect that as
models scale, the frontier of relevant research tasks will simply scale
with them. To empirically test this core hypothesis—that variance peaks
at the boundary of capability—we require a domain where difficulty can
be dialed continuously, evaluated cheaply, and repeated enough to
estimate spread with statistical confidence. Since our thirteen
long-horizon research tasks do not permit this, we use MAX-3-SAT on
random 3-CNF formulas: the number of variables sets the difficulty,
random assignment and a strong classical solver bracket the attainable
range, and freshly generated instances successfully rule out
memorization.

Figure 4: Outcome variance is largest at the frontier of what the model
can do. Spread vanishes where every run solves or fails the formula and
peaks in between.

Empirical evidence from MaxSAT problem. We run three open-weight models
(Qwen3.5-4B, 9B, and 27B) on random 3-CNF formulas with $`V`$ variables,
$`V`$ from 10 to $`100{,}000`$, and measure the number of unsatisfied
clauses $`u`$ of the best assignment each run produces. We normalize
this raw quantity into an attainment metric $`h`$, representing the
fraction of the performance gap closed between random guessing and a
strong classical solver. Specifically,
$`h=(u_{\text{random}}-u_{\text{agent}})/(u_{\text{random}}-u_{\text{ref}})`$,
where $`u_{\text{random}}\approx 6V/8`$ is the expected number of
unsatisfied clauses for a uniformly random assignment, and
$`u_{\text{ref}}`$ is the minimum $`u`$ found by a multi-restart WalkSAT
baseline. Thus, $`h=0`$ indicates performance equivalent to random
guessing, while $`h=1`$ indicates matching the WalkSAT reference
ceiling. We aggregate independent runs into evaluation cells defined by
a specific (model, $`V`$) pair, with each cell containing between 8 and
32 runs that differ only in their initial seed (32 at most sizes, 8 at
the smallest and largest formulas). For each cell, we compute the mean
attainment $`a`$, and the execution spread $`s`$, defined as the
population standard deviation. To quantify the uncertainty in $`s`$
arising from sample size, we compute $`95\%`$ confidence intervals via
bootstrapping, resampling the runs within each cell with replacement
$`2{,}000`$ times. As shown in
Figure [4](#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 6.2 What Drives Variance? ‣ 6 Analysis ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents"),
each point represents a single (model, problem size) pair, plotted
according to the fraction of the reference solver’s performance the
model attains (horizontal axis) and the variance among its runs
(vertical axis). Because difficulty is measured relative to model
capability rather than absolute problem size, the three models trace a
unified curve despite operating at different scales. Variance peaks when
a model achieves roughly half of the reference performance, collapsing
at both the trivial and intractable extremes. Fitting a least-squares
quadratic reveals a strict inverted-U relationship between attainment
and spread, peaking at $`a=0.497`$. This suggests that the observed
variance stems from genuine exploration of distinct idea basins,
providing the empirical signal that our _fork-and-flush_ algorithm
exploits.

## 7 Related Work

Autoresearch and Self-Improving Agents. Long-horizon agents ([Wijk et
al., 2024](#bib.bib30); [Chan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31)) are
increasingly used to drive open-ended research, from automated paper
writing ([Lu et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Schmidgall et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32)) to evolutionary program search ([Romera-Paredes et
al., 2024](#bib.bib27); [Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib7); [Lange et
al., 2025](#bib.bib33)) and autonomous experimentation ([Boiko et al.,
2023](#bib.bib36); [Swanson et al., 2025](#bib.bib37); [Gottweis et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib39)). In fact, the
research loop proposed by The AI Scientist ([Lu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1); [Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)) automates the
idea–experiment–writeup cycle, while AlphaEvolve ([Novikov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib7)) evolves programs against a grader over time. Beyond a
single run, LLM agents typically improve _across_ tasks either by
accumulating experience ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib8); [Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib9); [Zhou et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)) or by distilling
their own successful trajectories back into the model
parameters ([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib11); [Singh et al.,
2024](#bib.bib12); [Qu et al., 2024](#bib.bib13); [Falck et al.,
2026](#bib.bib35)). _Fork-and-flush_ is orthogonal to both paradigms as
it improves a single run _within_ one task, with no memory carried
across tasks and no weight updates. The only state that propagates
across branches is the workspace, as the intervention exists precisely
to clear the conversational context. To evaluate LLM agents in these
long-horizon settings, benchmarks such as Terminal-Bench ([Merrill et
al., 2026](#bib.bib14)) and
Terminal-Bench-Science ([Terminal-Bench-Science Team, 2026](#bib.bib15))
grade end-to-end terminal workflows on a strict pass/fail basis, while
Frontier-CS ([Mang et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)), EdgeBench ([Zhu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3)), and DiscoGen ([Goldie et al., 2026](#bib.bib34)) pose
open-ended algorithmic problems with graded, unbounded scores.

Test-Time Compute and Population-Based Search. _Go with the winners_
([Aldous and Vazirani, 1994](#bib.bib19)) keeps a population of
searchers and periodically replaces its weak members with copies of
strong ones. Population Based Training ([Jaderberg et al.,
2017](#bib.bib18)) applies the same exploit-and-perturb cycle to
neural-network training, where a worker copies a better worker’s weights
and then jitters its hyperparameters. Fork-and-flush is this scheme over
agents: the state copied is a workspace of files rather than a parameter
vector, and the perturbation is discarding the conversation that
produced those files — the fork must re-derive its intent from the
artifacts, which is what lets it land in a different basin. Successive
halving and racing algorithms ([Karnin et al., 2013](#bib.bib21))
likewise spend rounds of budget on a shrinking survivor set, which is
our selection step without the shared trunk; Go-Explore ([Ecoffet et
al., 2021](#bib.bib22)) archives promising states and returns to them
before exploring, the same return-to-the-best-workspace move our fan-out
makes. _West-of-N_ utilizes the best and worst candidates ([Pace et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17)) to generate preference pairs for self-improving
reward models. In tree search, MCTS ([Kocsis and Szepesvári,
2006](#bib.bib20)) grows a tree by expanding the nodes its interim value
estimates favour; Tree of Thoughts ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib23)) and
Language Agent Tree Search ([Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)) bring that
machinery to LLMs at the granularity of individual thoughts or actions.
Fork-and-flush searches the same way but coarser: a node is a whole
agent episode-chain over a workspace, expansion is a context-cleared
fork, and the value estimate is the task’s own grader — the granularity
at which long-horizon runs actually produce scores. Finally,
sampling-based test-time scaling — AlphaCode’s filtered mass generation
([Li et al., 2022](#bib.bib25)), repeated sampling ([Brown et al.,
2024](#bib.bib26); [Snell et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)), and evolutionary
program search ([Romera-Paredes et al., 2024](#bib.bib27)) — resamples
complete solutions from scratch, where fork-and-flush resamples
continuations of the best partial work so far.

Plateaus in Long Reasoning. Related forms of stalled exploration have
been observed in long-chain reasoning models. [Gema et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib40) construct tasks on which extending a model’s
reasoning reduces rather than improves accuracy. [Marjanović et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib42) find that DeepSeek-R1 repeatedly revisits previously
explored problem formulations, obstructing further exploration, while
[Pipis et al. (2026)](#bib.bib41) study a more extreme form of
repetition in which reasoning models fall into textual loops. Closest to
our setting, [Wen et al. (2025)](#bib.bib43) describe _tunnel vision_:
early mistakes commit a model to a suboptimal reasoning path, and
recovery becomes less likely as the erroneous prefix grows.

Our work complements these studies by examining the analogous phenomenon
in long-running autoresearch agents, which repeatedly modify executable
artifacts and receive external feedback over hours to several days. In
standard long-chain reasoning, each new token is conditioned on the
preceding reasoning trace, continually exposing the model to its earlier
choices. Our agents, however, periodically compact their conversational
histories, replacing the full trace with a summary of the progress so
far. One might expect this compaction to weaken dependence on the
earlier reasoning path and reopen exploration. We find that it is
insufficient: trajectories still plateau at substantially different
levels and remain localized in idea basins. _Fork-and-flush_ goes
further by starting parallel continuations with fresh chat contexts
while preserving the accumulated workspace.

## 8 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced _fork-and-flush_, a periodic intervention
designed to help autonomous research agents escape localized regions of
the solution space, which we term idea basins. We demonstrated that as
agents tackle open-ended problems by repeatedly proposing, evaluating,
and refining candidate solutions, independent runs often plateau at
substantially different scores—a high-variance bottleneck that persists
even with considerable additional compute. To overcome this,
_fork-and-flush_ forks the agent into parallel trajectories that each
inherit a copy of the accumulated workspace but begin with fresh chat
contexts. After exploring for a fixed horizon, the agent continues from
the highest-scoring branch. Across thirteen long-horizon research and
engineering tasks under an equal compute budget, _fork-and-flush_
consistently outperforms serial baselines, demonstrating that
fork-and-flush provides a practical path for scaling test-time compute
in autonomous agents. We present exciting avenues for future work.
First, the substantial computational expense and time required to
evaluate frontier LLMs on long-horizon agentic workflows inherently
limit the number of tasks we could practically include in this study.
Second, the branched trajectories currently operate independently
without coordination. Future work will investigate inter-agent
communication and role specialization across branches, as well as
scaling our evaluations to a broader suite of tasks and newly released
frontier models.

Figure [5](#A3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Appendix C Variance Analysis Plots ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")
illustrates eight independent single-run trajectories across four
embedded tasks. On high-variance problems such as polyomino (final
scores $`82.2`$–$`94.9`$), p150 ($`109.1`$–$`137.1`$), and AHC014
($`7.8`$–$`59.8`$), the runs clearly separate into distinct basins that
track their final performance. For instance, on AHC014, the two
highest-scoring runs share a single basin while all remaining runs fall
into another. In contrast, on a low-variance task like job-shop
($`7.2`$–$`10.8`$), the geometric structure is weak: the two basins
overlap heavily, and runs freely move between them. Because this basin
structure is poorly defined, we draw no basin-based claims from
job-shop.

## Appendix D Schedule Design

Fixed Schedule vs. Plateau Detection. The natural trigger for a
fork-and-flush round is a performance plateau. However, early
development runs using a stall-clock trigger rarely executed the
intervention: across five tasks, $`15`$ of $`25`$ plateau-triggered runs
exhausted their budget before the stall criteria were met. Dynamic
triggers proved practically difficult to tune for three reasons. First,
credit costs per step vary widely (e.g., $`6.1\times`$ variance across
tinyCIFAR runs), meaning a fixed credit threshold detects a stall
prematurely in some runs and entirely misses it in others. Second, tasks
often exhibit micro-improvements that restart the stall clock. This
allows runs creeping upward within a narrow local basin to evade
detection—the exact failure mode fork-and-flush is designed to fix.
Third, requiring a sufficiently long stall window (e.g., $`20\%`$ of the
budget) to ignore noise pushes the first intervention too late in the
trajectory. A fixed schedule resolves all three issues by guaranteeing
the intervention fires, standardizing the branch spend, and removing
task-dependent tolerance tuning.

Sensitivity to Cadence. While we did not systematically sweep all
schedule parameters, our development runs span three configurations
(Table [5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix D Schedule Design ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")):
the plateau trigger, a single forced round at $`50\%`$ of the budget,
and our main setting of two forced rounds at $`33\%`$ and $`66\%`$. Both
fixed schedules outperform the single-run baseline on all six tested
tasks, with neither strictly dominating (the two-round schedule wins on
four tasks, the one-round on two). The plateau trigger performed poorly
on AHC014 and p171 primarily because it never fired. Though sample sizes
are small, this suggests the performance gains are robust to the exact
cadence of the fixed schedule.

Sensitivity to Branch Count. We set the branch count to $`K{=}4`$.
Because the branch spend per round is fixed at
$`K\,b_{\text{explore}}`$, increasing $`K`$ requires either drastically
reducing the exploration budget per branch or running fewer rounds
entirely. We found that $`K{=}4`$ strikes a practical balance,
allocating roughly $`6\%`$ of the total budget to each branch—enough
depth to meaningfully develop a new idea—while preserving enough global
budget for multiple rounds of intervention. The minimal case of
$`K{=}1`$ corresponds to the flush-only ablation discussed in
Section [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Ablations: Impact of Forking and Flushing ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents").

| task      | single-run | plateau trigger        | one round at 50%        | rounds at 33/66%        |
| --------- | ---------- | ---------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------- |
| polyomino | $`87.54`$  | $`93.84`$ (1)          | $`\mathbf{94.43}`$ (1)  | $`93.82`$ (6)           |
| job-shop  | $`9.23`$   | $`\mathbf{11.44}`$ (1) | $`10.24`$ (2)           | $`10.99`$ (2)           |
| AHC014    | $`21.32`$  | $`21.30`$ (3)          | $`26.98`$ (4)           | $`\mathbf{40.97}`$ (5)  |
| p150      | $`118.24`$ | $`126.72`$ (4)         | $`\mathbf{145.13}`$ (2) | $`135.52`$ (7)          |
| p171      | $`83.70`$  | $`80.16`$ (4)          | $`85.83`$ (5)           | $`\mathbf{89.11}`$ (11) |

SOE

Figure 6:
Figure [3](#S6.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 6.1 Visualizing Escaping Idea Basins ‣ 6 Analysis ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")
under two embeddings of the same judged triplets. Top: t-STE, as in
Figure [3](#S6.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 6.1 Visualizing Escaping Idea Basins ‣ 6 Analysis ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents").
Bottom: SOE, aligned to the same frame, with basins recomputed on its
coordinates; $`99\%`$ of single-run artifacts keep their basin. In both,
the rejected branches ($`\times`$) stay in the branch point’s basin and
within about one median single-run step of it, while the selected branch

under t-STE and $`10\times`$ under SOE, in each case more than twice the

In
Section [6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Visualizing Escaping Idea Basins ‣ 6 Analysis ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents"),
we visualized idea basins using t-Distributed Stochastic Triplet
Embedding (t-STE) ([van der Maaten and Weinberger, 2012](#bib.bib28)).
To verify the robustness of our geometric findings, we refit the exact
same LLM-judged triplets using Soft Ordinal Embedding (SOE) ([Terada and
von Luxburg, 2014](#bib.bib4)).
Figure [6](#A5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix E Robustness of the Embedding Space ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")
presents a direct side-by-side comparison of the two embeddings for the
polyomino task. The top row reproduces the t-STE map and step distances
from
Figure [3](#S6.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 6.1 Visualizing Escaping Idea Basins ‣ 6 Analysis ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents"),
while the bottom row shows the SOE refit aligned to the same frame. 
Crucially, the qualitative behavior of the _fork-and-flush_ intervention
remains identical under the SOE geometry. The rejected branches
($`\times`$) remain trapped within the local basin of the fork point,
moving less than one median single-run step. Conversely, the selected
branch successfully jumps to a different idea basin. While the absolute
numerical magnitude of the jump scales down under SOE (from $`43\times`$
the median single-run step under t-STE to $`10\times`$ under SOE), it
remains definitively significant: the jump is still more than twice the
largest step any single-run baseline ever takes ($`4.1`$ units). This
confirms that the ability of _fork-and-flush_ to escape localized
plateaus is a genuine property of the search strategy that is robust to
the choice of embedding algorithm.

## Appendix F Artifact Embedding Methodology

Each idea-space map is produced in four stages:

(i) Subsampling. From every trajectory we retain the exact graded
submission artifacts, deduplicate identical files by content hash, and
select a fixed number of evenly spaced snapshots per run in order of
first occurrence ($`51`$ per run on every mapped task).

(ii) Specification. An LLM rewrites each sampled submission into a
canonical functional specification under a fixed section schema with an
exhaustive parameter table. The rewrite strips coding syntax and
stylistic signal—formatting, naming, how the file is organized—while
preserving the algorithm, data structures, and every numeric choice.
This ensures that a competent engineer who has never seen the file could
reimplement it from the specification alone and obtain materially the
same behavior and score. Judging specifications rather than raw source
keeps two artifacts edited from a common ancestor from being called
similar merely because they _read_ alike.

(iii) Triplet Comparison. An LLM judge answers ordinal queries—is anchor
$`a`$’s approach closer to $`b`$’s or to $`c`$’s?—over the
specifications, mixing within-run triplets with cross-condition anchors
balanced across conditions. The judge is the same LLM deployment that
wrote the specifications, so a single model accounts for every generated
token in the pipeline, and each map is built from $`6{,}375`$ judgments
($`5{,}610`$ on p150).

(iv) Embedding. We fit a two-dimensional t-STE embedding ([van der
Maaten and Weinberger, 2012](#bib.bib28)) to the judged rankings,
keeping the best of eight random restarts by training agreement. One in
five judged triplets per anchor is held out and never used in fitting;
Table [6](#A6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix F Artifact Embedding Methodology ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")
reports agreement on those held-out judgments.

|           |                 |       |          |       |          |
| --------- | --------------- | ----- | -------- | ----- | -------- |
|           |                 | t-STE |          | SOE   |          |
| task      | judged triplets | train | held out | train | held out |
| polyomino | 6,375           | 0.90  | 0.87     | 0.90  | 0.85     |
| AHC014    | 6,375           | 0.90  | 0.87     | 0.91  | 0.86     |
| p171      | 6,375           | 0.88  | 0.85     | 0.88  | 0.84     |
| p150      | 5,610           | 0.87  | 0.83     | 0.86  | 0.80     |
| job-shop  | 6,375           | 0.86  | 0.81     | 0.85  | 0.79     |
| _mean_    |                 | 0.88  | 0.85     | 0.88  | 0.83     |

Table 6: Held-out validation of the idea-space maps. Agreement is the
fraction of LLM triplet judgments the fitted two-dimensional map
reproduces; chance is $`0.50`$. t-STE is the embedding used in the
figures; SOE refits the same triplets with soft ordinal embedding.

Validation. Each map is fit on $`80\%`$ of the judged triplets and
scored on the remaining $`20\%`$; agreement
(Table [6](#A6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix F Artifact Embedding Methodology ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents"))
is the fraction of held-out judgments the two-dimensional coordinates
reproduce, with chance at $`0.50`$. The t-STE maps reach
$`0.81`$–$`0.87`$ (mean $`0.85`$) with a train–test gap of
$`0.03`$–$`0.05`$, so they generalise rather than memorise. Refitting
the same triplets with SOE, whose hinge loss does not inflate the gaps
between clusters, gives $`0.79`$–$`0.86`$ (mean $`0.83`$): a slightly
weaker fit, so t-STE is used for the figures and SOE as the check that
the displacements are not artefacts of its heavy-tailed kernel.
Agreement is lowest on job-shop, the task with the least outcome
variance and the weakest basin structure. Run membership alone
(“artifacts from the same run are closer”) reproduces only
$`0.52`$–$`0.60`$ of held-out judgments, so the maps capture more than
which run an artifact came from.

task’s budget, the point at which the table reads it. The grey band is

table uses, and the grey line is their median. The blue line is the
run’s best score so far. Each branch is drawn in its own colour from the
score it inherited at the fork, and every graded submission is a dot. A
star marks the branch adopted when a round closes, a cross each branch
that was dropped, and the shaded columns span the branch rounds. On
kernel and tinyCIFAR, some runs use a single forced round at $`50\%`$ of
the budget
(Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Schedule Design ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")).

## Appendix H Trajectories Across Idea Basins

To further illustrate how the intervention navigates the solution space,
Figure [8](#A8.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Appendix H Trajectories Across Idea Basins ‣ Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basinsin Autoresearch Agents")
visualizes nine distinct _fork-and-flush_ trajectories mapped onto their
respective task’s idea basins. The embeddings reveal three distinct
search behaviors. First, during the opening round, initial probes
frequently scatter across multiple basins (e.g., p171-fd2, ahc014-f2),
allowing the agent to evaluate fundamentally different structural
approaches before committing. Second, later in the run, flushes can
trigger a definitive jump into a new basin (as seen in poly-d4),
enabling the run to successfully escape a local optimum. Finally, even
when the flush does not induce a basin jump—and both rejected and
selected branches remain localized near the fork (e.g., ahc014-t1)—the
intervention still drives robust local refinement, consistently driving
the trajectory to final scores that surpass the single-run baselines.

## Appendix I Prompts

### I.1 Agent prompts

Every message an agent receives is either the task’s own packaging (its
statement, its AGENT.md workflow notes and its submission script) or one
of the texts below, which we wrote. No message in any condition states
the credit budget or how much of it remains; agents are never told how
much compute they have. The episode messages are logged verbatim with
every run.

Continuation message.. Sent at the start of every episode after the
first, in every condition (single-run, best-of-4 draws, fork-and-flush
trunks and branches), whenever the harness resumes a session:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Branch directive.. Appended to the first message of a directed branch in
a fork-and-flush round. In each round two of the $`K`$ branches carry
it; the others start from the same workspace with no directive:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The directive does not measurably change which branch wins: across the
$`178`$ mid-run rounds of the study, a directed branch was selected in
$`81`$ ($`46\%`$), against the $`50\%`$ expected if it had no effect
(two-sided binomial $`p{=}0.26`$). We therefore treat the directed and
undirected branches as interchangeable.

Protected-incumbent notice.. Appended to the first message of any
branch, or any resumed leg, that inherits a workspace containing a
scored submission. It exists because task scaffolds can overwrite the
canonical solution file, and it is the only place a score is quoted to
the agent:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Task wrappers.. For the EdgeBench tasks the first message is the text
below, followed by the original EdgeBench agent query:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

For LLM-SQL it is the text below, followed by the original task
statement:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

For sphere-pack we replaced the packaging’s pass/fail scoring line with
the first text below and added the second to its AGENT.md:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

All other instruction text is the task’s own packaging.
